svg.aria-label: AWS deployment pipeline end to end: secrets are written into the customer account at onboarding, then a single workflow run replicates images and performs one terraform apply that creates every remaining resource.

g.text: AWS — one tenant, from form submission to a running chatbot
Every tenant credential is already inside the customer's account before the run starts, so the run itself only ever carries references.
WHAT THE PLATFORM AND THE RUN DO, IN ORDER
WHAT EXISTS IN THE CUSTOMER'S AWS ACCOUNT
At onboarding, before any run exists
The platform assumes the customer's deployment role for fifteen minutes and
writes three secrets into their own Secrets Manager, keeping only the ARNs.
It also keeps its own encrypted copy of the signer secret, which it needs again later.
Secrets Manager, and nothing else yet
{slug}/llm-api-key · {slug}/docs-signer-secret
{slug}/pinecone-api-key, when the tenant chose Pinecone
No compute, no network and no storage exist at this point.
Notify the platform that the run started
Pull both golden images from the platform's own registry
Assume the tenant role and replicate both images into their registry
Ensure the ECS service-linked role exists
terraform init, against state held in the platform's bucket
Read the customer's Pinecone key from their Secrets Manager
Install the signer's Node dependencies
terraform apply — a single pass
Read the outputs and upload them as a run artifact
Notify the platform of the result
carries the run id and run URL, so the platform can poll this run later
the platform builds the chatbot once; no tenant image is ever built from source
the image the tenant runs is pulled from a registry they own, not from the platform's
a one-time account prerequisite that Terraform cannot create for itself
tenants/{slug}.tfstate — one state file per tenant, never shared
masked immediately, then handed to the provider; only when vector_store = pinecone
the Lambda's zip is built from disk during apply, so the modules must be there first
every remaining resource is created here, in one graph, with no ordering gap to bridge
a durable copy, so a lost callback costs one extra API call rather than the URLs
succeeded or failed, carrying the chatbot URL, the load balancer DNS and the signer URL
Elastic Container Registry, two repositories
{slug}/chatbot and {slug}/chatbot-frontend, each holding this deployment's version tag
the tasks defined below can only pull from here
Everything else, created by that one apply
VPC 10.20.0.0/16, two public subnets across zones, internet gateway
Application Load Balancer, a frontend target group and an /api/* rule to the backend
ECS cluster with a frontend service and a backend service, one task each
Execution role that may read the LLM secret ARN, and nothing else
Task role that may get and list the docs bucket, and nothing else
S3 documents bucket: encrypted, public access blocked, CORS for the platform origin
docs-signer Lambda and its function URL, with a put-and-delete-only role
CloudWatch log group for the tasks, fourteen-day retention
RDS PostgreSQL with pgvector and its connection secret — when that store was chosen
The apply resolves each secret ARN into the task definition. No secret value passes
through the runner at any point in this column.
A Pinecone index is created in the customer's own project instead, when that store was chosen.
What the platform knows when the run ends
The chatbot URL, the load balancer DNS name and the docs-signer URL, written onto the tenant row; the run id, run URL and terminal state, written onto the deployment row.
It holds no session, key or role into this account afterwards. To upload a document later it calls the signer URL with the shared secret it kept from onboarding.
If the final callback is lost, the platform recovers all three URLs from the run artifact uploaded at step 9.
The shape of this pipeline follows from one property of AWS: a tenant's secret store exists independently of the deployment, so it can be populated first and referenced later.
That is what allows a single apply and a run that never handles a customer credential. Compare the Azure pipeline, where neither holds.
